senses: A philosophy of architecture that has elements akin to feng shui
examples: Very few know that plants also improve the vastu of a place.

senses: An energetic, danceable style of music originating in Angola, combining local styles like semba with influences from Caribbean music, especially zouk and soca.
Someone or something which pleases.
ety: From Middle English plesere, equivalent to please + -er.

senses: The traditional garment worn by men and women in Madagascar, consisting of a rectangular length of cloth wrapped around the body.
examples: Wind stirred the grass, leaving streaks of gold-green light, and the patterns of lambas on women coming home from the market took on the vividness of a Degas painting.

senses: To tie again; to tie something that has already been tied or was tied before.
examples: She stopped walking for a moment to retie her shoe.

senses: A chain or ring to which a key may be attached.
An ornamental piece holding such a chain or ring.
That takes place on a sports field
Looking obliquely; having the vision distorted.
askew, not level
ety: Derived from asquint (“obliquely, with a sidelong glance”).

senses: The conductor or leader of the dramatic chorus in Ancient Greece.
The chief or leader of a party or interest.
ety: From Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader”), from κορυφή (koruphḗ, “head”).
examples: In this work Homer and Virgil already appear beside Cicero and Plato as doctrinal authorities. The four corypheuses are infallible; any contradiction between them is wholly out of the question.
That noted corypheus of the Independent faction.
Then Corypheus Marat, author of the Friend of the People, constantly denounced him as the traitor Lafayette.

senses: Pulsating; that pulses.
Characterized by pulses.
Of a musical instrument: played by striking or beating.
ety: From Medieval Latin pulsātilis, Latin pulsō + -ilis.
examples: The Conglomerate itself was a pulsatile labyrinth of muscle, gelatinous pockets and hanging ganglion.

senses: Someone skilled in phytology; a writer on plants; a botanist.
A modern or revived form of paganism; modern pagan religion.
A vineyard or wine estate, especially in France.
ety: From French domaine (“zone, estate”). Doublet of domain.

senses: Someone who makes a wish
ety: From Middle English wyssher, wisscher, wyshere, equivalent to wish + -er.

senses: The right to rations at court, granted to the king's household, attendants etc.
Eruca spp., especially Eruca sativa (syn. Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa)
Diplotaxis tenuifolia
ety: Probably from a Southern Italian dialect word equivalent to Standard Italian rucola, whence also, since c. 1967, English rucola. Also cognate to rocket (“plant”), eruca, roquette.

senses: An ancient monument consisting of a typically raised stone with a runic inscription.
A small tile-shaped stone or tablet with a single rune inscribed on it, used for divinatory and esoteric purposes.
A quarter or district of an urban settlement in France.
ety: Borrowed from French quartier. Doublet of quarter.

senses: Of, or like a baby; infantile
That is able to be condensed; that can undergo condensation
To absorb (something) again.
To undergo resorption.
ety: From Latin resorbere, from re- (“again”) + sorbere (“to suck in”).

senses: A prayer, typically beginning “I confess to Almighty God…” in English, in which public confession of sins is made.
ety: From Latin cōnfiteor (“to confess”), the first word of the prayer and used as its title in Ecclesiastical Latin. Doublet of confess.

senses: An adherent of one of the forms of intellectualism.
The pin that attaches a connecting rod to a crank.
examples: Three independent sets of Walschaerts valve gear are provided, those for the outside cylinders being driven by return cranks placed on the driving crankpins, and by crosshead arms attached to the crossheads.

senses: A biennial plant, Pastinaca sativa, related to the carrot.
The root of the parsnip, when used as a vegetable.
ety: From 16th-century parsnepe, from Middle English passenep, a modification of Old French pasnaie by influence of Middle English nepe (“turnip”), from Latin pastināca (“parsnip, carrot”), from pastinum (“two-pronged fork”) as in pastināre (“to dig up the ground”).. The irregular intrusive r may be due to influence from parsley.

senses: A utensil for removing the core from apples and similar fruit or vegetables.
A dish of fish (or sometimes chicken) first fried then marinated in a spiced vinegar and served cold.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish escabeche, from Andalusian Arabic اَلسُّكَّبَاج (assukkabáj), from Arabic اَلسِّكْبَاجَة (as-sikbāja), feminine of سِكْبَاج (sikbāj), from Middle Persian [script needed] (*sḵbʾk' /⁠*sikbāg⁠/) (whence Persian سکبا (sekbâ)). Possibly related to ceviche. Doublet of caveach and sikbaj.

senses: A soapmaker.
An astronomical object, approximately the size of the Moon, formed from the mutual gravitational attraction of planetesimals; they are thought to collide with each other and slowly form planets
A lake or long, narrow inlet, especially in Ireland.
ety: Borrowed from Irish loch (from Old Irish loch), from Proto-Celtic *loku (“lake, pool”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“pond, pool”). Doublet of lay, loch, and Looe.

senses: An advocate of reductionism.
To cause diffraction
To undergo diffraction
ety: From Latin diffractus (“past participle of diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”)”).

senses: An Italian apéritif.
ety: From Italian aperitivo. Doublet of aperitive and apéritif.

senses: The use of a paramilitary force.
The recreational drug 4-methylmethcathinone, related to cathinone.
A fine blizzard of snow in Russia.
ety: From Russian пурга́ (purgá), from a Finnic source such as southern Karelian purgu or Veps purg (“snowstorm”).
examples: When the black purga blows it can pile the snow higher than a ship's mast overnight.

senses: The state or sphere of those who are single (unmarried or unattached).
A stew associated with the Liverpool area, usually containing (at least) meat, onions, carrots and potatoes.
ety: Clipping of lobscouse, of uncertain origin.

senses: To refine (something) until it disappears or loses all meaning.
To raise (someone) to a high office or status; to dignify, to elevate, to exalt.
To raise something to a state of excellence; to improve.
Synonym of sublime (“to become higher in quality or status; to improve”).
ety: From Middle English sublymate, from Latin sublīmātus, past participle of sublīmāre (“to raise, elevate”).

senses: Producing grunts.
ety: From Middle English gruntynge (“grunting”); equivalent to grunt + -ing.
